reflectiveLogbook.reflection:
Today was my first day at revenue department, it was less about collecting data and more about to make myself familiar to the office register which is called Field Entry. I was conscious when I was introduced with the Supervisor, that introduction was sociolinguistics evidence rather than a procedural information. I have observed the language which is used with me was more formal and structured as compare to the language used with the staff member. This reminded me the concept of Audience Design by Bell, which tell that speaker structure its code and formality according to who is listening.
Later, my supervisor instructed me that which areas and section of the office are accessible for me and which are not. At first, I thought it is completely administrative instruction but later it reflected the concept of domain of power by Tariq Rahman. This is where the department has sets it boundaries between what can be shared with an outsider and which will restricted within the hierarchy of the department. These boundaries are not neutral it describes where the power and information are concentrated. 
I was completely surprised how much could be learned from linguistically from the short routine introduction. I get great evidence of sociolinguistics as started formally logging interactions. I had not recorded it in the structured way. Tomorrow I will apply speaking framework in real time rather than just noticing the details.

Today, it was less observing the language nut more about to build the apparatus which will help me to give some sensible meaning to tomorrow’s observation. I have sketched the organogram. it will verify my claim about a language choice between group of people. It has made clear that who is official, staff and a visitor so I can be confused later. The organogram will help me to say with confidence that why there is register shift between two participants.
I was building up the terminology book which led me to think clearly about the Fishman’s Domain which bell discussed how language choice cluster around setting, topic and participants. By building this structure before collecting any data will help me to implement theoretical framework into practical day to day routine.  
I have realized that this office interacts and communicates with public in many different ways. These interactions involve different language and different styles of speaking. I want to observe these interactions carefully. For that purpose, from tomorrow I will immediately record every detail rather to wait till the end of day so I may not forget any details.

Today it was my first exposure to public dealing. I made a conscious effort to notice that who gets addressed in which language. If a visitor comes in urban dress, then it would be addressed in Urdu with some mixture of English terms. In contrast, when person comes in rural dress then they would be addressed in Sindhi language. It Is the real example of audience design. Before choosing any code, officials read the social cues.
I have also noticed the clear register gap between the conversation among staff and the conversation between staff ad visitor. With visitor conversation is more explanatory and detailed while the staff conversation has shared meaning that is why it is short and clipped. This indicates the register variation, as Allen Bell suggested. The same official communicates with two people with different register which is completely related to audience and purpose.
Tomorrow, I have to be careful about generalizing my observation. My observation should be suggestive not conclusive.

This week, I focused on times when a speaker went from one code to another mid-sentence in their conversation in order to use Sindhi, Urdu, or sometimes English words. Several of these switches seemed to focus on technical or procedural terminology: an official would start explaining something to a visitor in Sindhi and then move into Urdu or English only for procedural terminology, like the concepts only existed in that language or code. It was similar to what Bell described code-switching as a deliberate and meaningful action rather than a random and carefree mixture of languages.
Also, today I focused on noticing how the visitors and officials used politeness strategies in their conversations. There were a lot of softened requests, indirect language and addressing the visitors in a polite way, especially the old or anxious-looking ones. It made me realize the role of face management in these conversations something that would have gone unnoticed if I tracked only vocabulary. The language at the counter does much more than just transmitting information from official to visitor.
Next week, I would like to make my coding of code-switches more precise. On day one, I observed that there was a change but not necessarily the word or issue that led to the change. On the next few days, however, I will make sure to note the exact word or issue that leads to the code-switch, whether that be a change in subject, person, emotion, etc., so that my final analysis of code-switching will be based on specific instances and not just the fact that code-switching “happens a lot.”

Reading through actual samples of written notices and forms has provided me with a very different type of data as compared to the spoken observation I have been conducting up until now. The register used in the written sample is very dense, formulaic, and makes use of vocabulary that is derived from Persian and Arabic, something which I have rarely heard being used in any of the spoken observations I have recorded during the last few days. Seeing the difference in the written form makes one realize how important the corpus-based aspect of the internship is.
However, adding to the notebook of terminology today also allowed me to see how many of these written terminologies seemed to need to be verbally translated into something more comprehensible before an average person could actually do anything about them. The notice would use some bureaucratic term without any further clarification, and it is only during the actual interaction at the counter that people actually get to know what they have to do. This relates to the idea by Rahman, whereby some bureaucratic language used in official spheres of activity may not be accessible to all those involved in the process.
This also caused me to rethink another point that I had raised on Day 1 regarding boundaries in documentation and what they say about the location of institutional power. It is not only about what kinds of documents I am allowed to access but also about how comprehensible those documents are to a regular visitor.

Today’s observation focused on seeing how officials actually define a technical term after a visitor is confused, instead of just observing that such explanations take place. The most prevalent approach I witnessed was one involving the repetition of ideas using simpler phrases, with the use of examples following, instead of the giving of a formal definition. There were some officials who even used a different code for the simplified explanation, even if the previous explanation had been in Urdu. This seems to be a classic case of accommodation, with officials not only choosing their words but the actual code as well.
This related to an observation made on Day 5. The register gap in the notices between writing and speaking is not simply a static gap that is left unresolved but is being crossed in real time via the interpretative work done by the staff which never gets recorded in any document. If I were to analyze only the written notices, I would find that the communication at the office was inaccessible; but seeing the way things have happened today, I realize that accessibility has been achieved via the spoken interaction process.

Today was less about observation and more about action than I initially anticipated. Having to use certain language for a minor but authorized project gave me an appreciation of how much institutional language is simply an unconscious carryover and reiteration of the past, and not something which is actively considered each time institutional language is used. So far I have seen the official language I have been cataloguing as something that was actively selected by officials for each communication, somewhat like style. But today really made me question that assumption, since most of the language is convention that is repeated through the office's written documents.
This is an important correction to make before I proceed further into the analysis, since this will influence my discussion about "the reason" why the register is constructed in such a way. It's not so much "officials opt for the formal language as a means of asserting their authority," but rather "officials receive the formal language, as it's always been done in this particular institution." I would like to consult the supervisor regarding the origin of some of the phrasing, whether it's mandated or just traditional practice.

The process of consolidating my terminology notebook for the week proved to be an important indicator of how well I have been doing at maintaining the quality of my data. Upon checking my notes, I noticed some words that I had recorded down which were my paraphrasing of what had actually been said in the office and not the actual word-for-word usage of the term. This is something that should be addressed, because if I do not, I would be creating my own glossary and not the actual one of the office.
Having reviewed the week’s work with the supervisor was also very productive. There were a few terms that I thought would only be used in a formal sense, but there were colloquial expressions associated with those terms as well, which I didn’t know about until now. Overall, this week’s experience has shown me that the process of checking terminology cannot be a one-time deal reserved for the end because minor mistakes accumulate fast if I don’t correct them on the go.

By charting the linguistic usage within the entire office rather than at the front desk alone, I was able to get a much clearer idea of the language usage within the office than before. The internal language used among employees used was more inclined towards Sindhi and informal Urdu, whereas any writing or upward communication used more of formal Urdu and English only in case of official titles or procedures. This trend is consistent with the one observed by Rahman where English and formal Urdu were used in power spheres despite being surrounded by a predominantly Sindhi environment.
Seeing it laid out all throughout the office in its entirety rather than observing it in isolated instances at the counter helped me realize that the trend seemed to be more of an institutional aspect than the choice of a select few individuals. That is a significant shift in my thinking process as well from saying "this particular officer favors Urdu" to saying "the institutional structure itself appears to classify languages according to their status and function

With regard to the specific act of code-switching within my observations this week, I attempted to move beyond just identifying that the action took place, and recording instead what I thought triggered it each time. The most common trigger by far that I identified was clarification, with second being emphasis on a particular instruction for the visitor to follow. The rapport building cases of code-switching were less common, but notable; the switching tended to occur when an official spoke in Sindhi with an older visitor, after initiating the interaction in Urdu.
It's changing the way I am thinking about code switching in the context of this institution in general. I began the internship thinking that it was sort of one thing, but I have come to see it more as a small kit of tools that officials can use to accomplish different communicative purposes according to whatever is needed at any particular point. The difference between those purposes seems to be going to make a big difference in how I will write about it.

When comparing formal announcements, spoken office discourse with the public, and informal staff discourse all together, I have been able to see the register contrast more clearly than before, when I was analyzing them individually each day. Formal announcements make use of lengthy vocabulary that is derived from Persian-Arabic administration, and there is hardly any switching of code at all. In the case of spoken office discourse with the public, it becomes softer, using more Sindhi as well as explanations. On the other hand, informal staff discourse gets rid of all the formal vocabulary, and makes use of contextual phrases.
The fact that these three registers are aligned in a sequence makes me believe that it might be more fitting to think of them as part of a continuum of formality rather than three entirely different things that I have been dealing with separately. The former would be a much more precise representation of how things stand compared to thinking of “formal” and “informal” as two distinct and unrelated categories.

Looking back at my notes for the past two weeks, the obvious trend that stands out from all my observations is that the choice of language in this case does not solely depend on one of these three aspects but on a combination of them all. The choice of the code used by an official for discussing one and the same topic varies according to who is listening and the level of formality of the situation.
The process of writing this paper helped me realize how much of my own interpretation I have unconsciously included in my observations in the last two weeks. For this reason, I have formulated specific questions to ask my supervisor about how I understand some of these patterns, specifically the rapport building code-switching observed on Day 10, as compared to how an insider to the institution understands them. This seems like an appropriate step before proceeding to the next stage of the internship, since it is better to make corrections now, instead of later in the report.

This day witnessed the start of the teaching phase of my internship experience. It is worth mentioning that unlike the previous days in which I had been watching the use of language in a corporate environment, on this day, I was working directly with the students. The classes that were allocated to me differed from each other because the school did not have a fixed schedule for my classes.
Before embarking on the lessons, I conducted an informal discussion with the students to ask them what they need and the topics they have covered before. I found out that some of them had already been exposed to syntax and morphology before by some interns who taught them earlier. Instead of revisiting the same topic, I opted to cover some other topics. In retrospect, I would say that this informal discussion can be compared to needs analysis in language teaching. Though not a formal survey or assessment, it enabled me to assess their needs and what would benefit them.
Regarding the lower classes, I concentrated my effort in introducing them to the idea of language and its significance and influence in the society. I started with introducing them to the four fundamental skills in language: listening, speaking, reading and writing. In addition to that, I talked about the fact that language can be used to communicate ideas and ideologies within the society, as well as gender roles and social beliefs. At the same time, I introduced them to the four parts of speech: nouns, pronouns, adjectives and verbs.
In terms of the more advanced classes, I introduced some sociolinguistic themes that could not be covered in the elementary classes. The themes were those of the link between language and society, language imperialism, and language as part of national identity. One issue that I raised in this connection was that of promoting Urdu as the language of national unity in Pakistan, allowing for the examination of the link between language policy, national identity, and language diversity. Another theme that I raised in class was the link between language and gender issues.
From my personal experience, I could relate the approach to differentiated instruction, which implies tailoring content and explanation of it based on learners' prior knowledge and level. Moreover, I can associate this experience with such concepts as critical language awareness and critical pedagogy that are discussed in relation to language, ideology, gender, and power issues. From the perspective of critical approaches, learners are to question the way in which language works in the society rather than consider it as something neutral or detached from society. Nevertheless, I admit that the introduction of critical issues is only a first step because the development of critical thinking of learners needs additional explanations and examples, as well as expression of their opinions.
In general, the first teaching day helped me realize that classroom teaching goes beyond presenting information. In addition to presentation, it is necessary to listen to learners, identify their prior knowledge, and make decisions concerning the content to teach them. On future days, I would like to improve my approach to organizing classroom explanations and increase involvement of learners in learning activities.

The current class built on the previous day’s lesson on language and society. In accordance with the students’ request, I concentrated more on the interrelation of such phenomena as language, power, gender, history and identity. I did not consider them separately but rather discussed how they are connected and what impact they have on the way the individual perceives himself and the society around him.
The major point that we talked about was the connection of language and power. In particular, I highlighted the fact that language is not only a communicative tool but that it can demonstrate social power, influence public discourse and present certain ideas in a particular way. In doing this, I mentioned the term language ideology that denotes the way the people view languages and their social value. The connection of this term to the influence of national ideology and history of Pakistan was also discussed.
I further talked about the history of India–Pakistan relations and the impact that history and historical events may have on national identity perception. In turn, this topic gave way to the problem of identity issues in Pakistan. Within Applied Linguistics, this issue may be linked with linguistic identity because language may serve as a tool of expression of the sense of belonging, cultural background, and social identity of an individual or a community. Moreover, this question touches upon the representation of different linguistic communities in the framework of national identity.
Furthermore, the link between language and gender was discussed. Language is embedded in social institutions and may mirror the expectations regarding male and female roles. The choice of words and addressing may indicate some features of gender relations within society.
In retrospect, I realize that today’s lecture could be linked to both critical language awareness and critical pedagogy, which emphasize that learners should investigate the connection between language and issues such as power, ideology, and structures rather than taking every representation at face value. Moreover, the lecture revealed a crucial point in that there is a difference between national identity and personal experiences, in that every single person or linguistic group may not perceive their identity in exactly the same manner.
Today’s class has made me realize the significance of using learner-centered approach. As the students themselves have asked for these topics, I could respond to their needs and desires rather than just move on with the pre-planned grammar classes. Nonetheless, I understood the necessity of carefully explaining the issue and giving a balanced example when it comes to discussing history, ideology and identity. Next time, I would be glad to tie up these discussions with language by means of analyzing how national identity and social groups are presented in textbooks, political speeches, general statements and everyday conversation.
In any case, today’s class made me see that Applied Linguistics could help me discuss certain issues which go beyond grammar and language teaching. It gives me the opportunity to analyze the role language plays in the process of identity formation, power display and social beliefs reproduction.

The present day experience in teaching was especially intriguing because many topics I taught were defined through the questions and requirements of the students. During one lesson a student asked me how we learn a language in general. I saw this as a chance to go not only for language teaching but also teach some basic theories of SLA as well. I described such theories as Behaviourism, Innatism and Sociocultural theory connected with Vygotsky. Through these theories I conveyed the ideas that learning a language may be viewed from different angles – experience and reinforcement, human nature of language and the importance of interaction.
This lesson made me understand the significance of connecting my teaching at classes with the theoretical knowledge I gained through my Applied Linguistics studies. Instead of teaching how to learn English, I taught different theories of how people acquire languages. Especially Sociocultural theory allowed me to talk about the importance of interaction, guidance and social environment in the process of acquiring language. This can be also connected with scaffolding – when learners get help and become capable of performing the same tasks on their own.
Another lesson in another class involved continuing the discussion on sociolinguistics, following the previous lessons which involved discussions about language, society, power, gender, and identity. The continuity of the topics gave me the opportunity to discuss more about the theme instead of making each class about an isolated topic. I was starting to realize how these topics could be discussed in the classroom and linked to the experiences of the students.
A request for a lesson on tenses in a lower level class made me create a table wherein all the tenses are listed for clarification and understanding. Rather than explaining the information about the tenses in a long discussion, I made use of a visual presentation to illustrate the grammatical information.
I attempted to include classroom communication in my teaching process as well. I made sure that my students participated in the lesson through one of the tasks rather than just listening to me explaining things. In this case, I see some similarity to Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) that focuses on meaningful communication and Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT), in which learners communicate in order to complete a certain task or achieve a specific goal. In addition, I would say that critical pedagogy plays a role in my teaching practice in general, especially when my students start asking questions and participate in discussion actively. At the same time, I understand that such teaching strategies depend on how the task is organized.
One of the most encouraging comments came from those students who expressed appreciation of the way I was explaining the lesson. Some even asked me about when I will come back and asked me to give another lesson. Moreover, they said that they liked the way we interacted in the classroom and felt that my teaching style was somewhat different. It encouraged me because it proved that my students were comfortable talking to me and interested in keeping up the studying process. However, I know that such kind of encouragement cannot be considered as an evidence of the way my students learn; it is important to see how they will perform during further lessons.
I understood today that flexible approach is essential for effective teaching. One can come into the classroom having one specific theme but can get another direction thanks to questions of learners. Also, I realized that different themes should be explained differently. Theoretical things may be discussed while grammar issues may be presented visually. I want to organize my tasks in the way which will be more effective in the next sessions so that I could evaluate whether my students could apply their knowledge.

This week's lesson was especially important as there were opportunities to introduce and use two teaching methods namely Critical Pedagogy and Task-Based Language Teaching. These methods were introduced in both higher and lower levels of classes with the adjustment of the explanation depending on the context of the classroom. The aim was to go beyond the teaching process where the students receive only the information and motivate them to get involved in questions and expressing their opinion.
Firstly, I introduced the idea of the Critical Pedagogy method paying special attention to the criticism of the banking model of education put forward by Paulo Freire. I elaborated on the banking model, where the teacher is seen as the one who has knowledge and simply deposits it in the heads of students that have to absorb and memorize it. Secondly, I introduced the idea of the critical pedagogy as a contrast to the banking model, which assumes that learners can independently think, question the information and be active in their learning.
Another issue that I wanted students to know is that education should not limit itself to memorizing what a teacher teaches. In addition to it, it is necessary for a learner to develop a skill of questioning, analyzing and forming his own understanding. The notion mentioned above is connected with the term of conscientization, introduced by Freire, and meaning a development of critical consciousness about social reality. Thus, it could be said that this time I had a possibility to show my students that they can take an active part in their education process and do not have to rely only on the teacher.
In addition to using Critical Pedagogy, I also applied TBLT into the lesson. I asked my students to perform certain tasks and share their answers in front of the class. In such way, I provided the students with the opportunity to participate in the lesson through interaction instead of explaining everything to them. This idea is connected with TBLT, since in this method learners use language to achieve a certain task.
The application of these approaches in the higher and lower classes assisted me in the realisation that one teaching approach can have different interpretations based on the level of the learners. The theoretical approach to the Banking Model needed to be illustrated using classroom activities and exercises. In the same vein, the activities created room for the learners to express their ideas in their own language.
The day's lesson has also enabled me to understand the difference between explaining the teaching methodologies and implementing them. Explaining what Critical Pedagogy meant to the learners was not enough. I had to provide them with a chance to reflect on the role of the teacher, their engagement and the creation of knowledge in the classroom. As well, providing an activity was an avenue for engaging in active learning, but I came to realise that the task should have clear goals and outcomes in the future.
In summary, the lesson helped me learn about the practical ways in which Critical Pedagogy and Task-Based Language Teaching could help in creating an interactive learning environment. This lesson made me think about the issues of guidance on the part of the teacher and autonomy on the part of the learner. In my future lessons, I hope to create some tasks and discussion forums where students can voice their opinions and ask questions.
